title: Burlington Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Burlington wells have a 310-foot median depth, strong reported yields, and finished well costs of about $16,800-$29,000.
h1: What Burlington, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Burlington means looking closely at the well record, not just asking if a property has water. Permits within five miles show a mostly deep plains-sediment setting, with the Ogallala and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers appearing most often. Reported wells commonly produce useful household and stock supplies, but construction details, static water level, and testing still matter on the individual parcel.

This guide uses Colorado DWR permit records for Burlington in Kit Carson County. The records include older wells, incomplete reports, and different uses, so they are useful for setting expectations and pricing a project—not for guaranteeing what a new hole will produce.

sections.heading: Burlington wells are usually about 310 feet deep
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Burlington is 310 feet. The middle half runs from 285 to 328 feet, which gives a driller a fairly tight starting range for a normal bid. About 66% of the depth records fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 34% fall between 100 and 300 feet. No recorded wells fall under 100 feet or above 600 feet in the depth mix, although the deepest individual record reaches 905 feet.

These depths fit Burlington’s plains setting, where alluvium and plains sedimentary rock are the stated drilling conditions. Permits name the Ogallala on 355 wells and an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer on 334. A site-specific driller should still review nearby logs before fixing casing, grout, and drilling depth.

sections.heading: Most Burlington production wells report useful flow
sections.html:
Among the 190 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 26.5 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 20.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute. That is a strong local result for ordinary household, stock, and many irrigation uses, but it is a reported well-yield figure rather than a promise for a new hole.

The records show 93% of reported yields above 15 gallons per minute, 6% between 5 and 15, and 1% between 1 and 5. None are listed under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the original pumping test, pump setting, recovery information, and permitted use. An exempt household-use well also remains subject to its permit conditions and the state’s 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels near Burlington deserve a closer look
sections.html:
The median static water level is 190 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 169 to 224 feet. That affects pump depth, electrical planning, and the cost of getting water into a house. A buyer should distinguish static water level from total well depth: a 310-foot well does not mean the water stands at 310 feet.

The decade comparison points to a deeper measured water level over time. The median was 166 feet below surface in the 1960s and 234 feet in the 2020s. This suggests a declining water table in the available measurements, but the series combines different locations and well conditions. Have a driller measure the actual well and review nearby records before relying on a trend for one property.

sections.heading: Burlington’s permit history shows a long drilling record
sections.html:
The local record covers 700 permitted wells, including 321 recorded as constructed and 417 with a total depth. Permits were issued in every decade shown, with the most activity in the 2000s at 116 permits. The newest permit year is 2025, so Burlington still has current well activity rather than only legacy construction.

For older and newer records combined, the most frequently named drillers are Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) with 119 records, Parrish Drilling (Parrish, Wayne) with 101, and Hilt, Fred Jr with 30. Those names help identify local drilling history. They do not replace a current bid, license check, or discussion of access and site conditions.

sections.heading: What a new Burlington well may cost
sections.html:
In Burlington’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses about $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 310 feet, the drilled hole works out to approximately $10,800 to $17,000. That is the hole itself, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $16,800 to $29,000. A written estimate should state what happens if the hole must go deeper, how casing and grout are priced, and what is included in trenching and power work. Keep separate allowances for house plumbing, treatment, access, and any septic or site-development work.

sections.heading: PFAS, septic, and dry-hole questions still matter
sections.html:
Strong area-wide yield numbers do not eliminate parcel-level risk. The mapped area within about ten miles includes 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are no historic mine features mapped in that area. Before closing, obtain a current water test suited to the property and ask whether the well lies near a known site or other potential source.

Also confirm the well’s construction, pump performance, and water quality rather than relying on a neighbor’s result. A low-producing or dry hole is possible even where nearby wells perform well. Septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, and the house location can constrain the build. Water rights may also require an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: A practical plan for buying or building near Burlington
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby DWR permits by depth, aquifer, yield, static level, and construction status. A property with a recorded well should have the permit, completion report, pump information, and a recent flow and water-quality test available for review. If the records are incomplete, price the uncertainty rather than assuming the median applies.

For vacant land, have a licensed driller evaluate the proposed house site, access route, power path, septic layout, and likely drilling location together. Burlington’s reported 310-foot median and 190-foot median static level are useful planning markers, while the $16,800-$29,000 finished-well model gives a starting budget. Confirm current permit and water-right requirements with Colorado DWR before construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Burlington, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Burlington is 310 feet. The middle half runs from 285 to 328 feet, and 66% of the depth records are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 905 feet. A nearby permit log is still the best guide for an individual lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Burlington, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 310-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $10,800-$17,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $16,800-$29,000. Ask what the bid includes and how deeper drilling is charged.

faq.q: How much water do Burlington wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 190 Burlington-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 26.5 gallons per minute and the middle half is 20.0-50.0 gallons per minute. Reported yields above 15 gallons per minute account for 93%. These figures describe existing reports, not a guarantee for a new well or a particular pump.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Burlington, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from yield or depth alone. The mapped area includes 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the property’s water tested before purchase and after construction, and review the well location against known environmental information. Treatment decisions should follow the test results.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Burlington, Colorado?
faq.a: The available decade data shows median measured water levels changing from 166 feet below surface in the 1960s to 234 feet in the 2020s. That pattern suggests deeper water levels over time, but the records come from different wells and locations. Measure the subject well and compare nearby logs before drawing a parcel-specific conclusion.
